earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached
earlier_scan.source_named: Ejeba, Salem Ochala. 2017. A grammar of Ígálâ. Port Harcourt: M & J Grand Orbit (xx+249pp); also Omachonu, G.S. 2001. Igala Phonetics and Phonology: An Overview. Univ. of Nigeria MA thesis. Neither online.

sources.citation: Adeniyi, Kolawole. 2017. The limits of perception in the tonal orthographies of three-tone systems. Linguistik Online 84(5), section 2.3 'Igala' (pp. 10-11). DOI 10.13092/lo.84.3844
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Gives Igala's 28 consonants and 7 vowels (after Ejeba 2009) and states 'Igala contrasts three tone heights, H, M, and L', with contour tones derived by assimilation (falling L after H, rising H after L, citing Akinkugbe 1978). The word 'stress' does not occur in the article.

sources.citation: Fresco, Edward M. 1969. The tones of the Yoruba and Igala disyllabic noun prefix. Journal of West African Languages 6(1): 31-34
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Scan scanned (no text layer). Compares tone combinations on VCV nouns in Igala and Yoruba (e.g. Igala una 'fire', oma 'child'); no mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the four pages.

sources.citation: Ejeba, Salem Ochala. 2023. Igala concord system. Journal of West African Languages 50 (Golden Jubilee edition): 85-103
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Morphosyntax paper. Only note on prosody: high tone marked with acute, low with grave, mid unmarked; subject clitics are tonally underspecified. No mention of stress.

sources.citation: Momoh, Mahmud. 2023. Vowels and the Igala language resources. Proceedings of the Fourth Workshop on Resources for African Indigenous Languages (RAIL 2023), ACL. DOI 10.18653/v1/2023.rail-1.12
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Non-linguist lexicographic note; calls Igala 'a tone-based language' and proposes an ad-hoc diacritic system (five 'tones', long vowels 'stressed with falling tones'); no rule for word stress and not a reliable phonological description.

sources.citation: Arokoyo, Bolanle Elizabeth. 2020. Studying the phonology of the Olukumi, Igala, Owe and Yoruba languages: a comparative analysis. Dialectologia 25: 45-58. DOI 10.1344/dialectologia2020.25.3
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Segmental (consonant/vowel/syllable) comparison based on the Ibadan 400 wordlist; no discussion of tone or stress at all.

sources.citation: Udaa, J. I. & J. A. Aliyu. 2019. Aspects of phonological constraints on the English of Igala students in selected schools in Kogi State, Nigeria. Ianna Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies 1(1): 1-23
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lists Igala phonemes (7 vowels) for contrast with English; nothing on Igala stress, tone or suprasegmentals.

sources.citation: Are, Olushola Bamidele & Hope Akinola. 2017. About the substitution of the voiceless post-alveolar affricate among Igala speakers of English. Linguistique et Langues Africaines 3: 11-28. DOI 10.4000/lla.11465
sources.note: L2-English study; no statement on Igala tone or stress (only a footnote that diacritics mark tone and nasalisation). Bibliography cites Silverstein 1973 and Akinkugbe 1978 as the Igala phonology sources.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Igala language' (phonology section; cites Omachonu 2001, Rodriguez 2014 academia.edu/7951455, Arokoyo 2020, Are & Akinola 2017)
sources.note: Secondary: lists consonants, 7 oral and 5 nasal vowels and 'five tones' (extra high, high, mid-high, mid, low); no mention of stress. Rodriguez 2014 (academia.edu) could not be reached by automated download and was not read.

sources.citation: Armstrong, Robert G. 1965. Comparative wordlists of two dialects of Yoruba with Igala. Journal of West African Languages 2(2): 51-78
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Scan; only the introduction (pp. 51-52) was scanned. Wordlist from an Enjema-dialect speaker (Okaba, Ankpa area); transcription 'not fully phonemic'; tones marked; nothing on stress in the introduction.

sources.citation: Philpot, W. T. A. 1935. Notes on the Igala Language. Bulletin of the School of Oriental Studies 7(4): 897-912
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: publisher DOI, paywalled; library e-access not checked
sources.note: Earliest grammatical sketch; p. 897 (seen) describes tones; the remaining 15 pages (paywalled) may comment on accent or emphasis.

sources.citation: Ejeba, Salem Ochala. 2016. A Grammar of Igala. Port Harcourt: M & J Grand Orbit Communications. Chapter 'Igala Phonology', pp. 23-78 (also 2017 print ed., xx+249 pp; PhD version 2016, University of Port Harcourt)
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: online with a university library login
sources.note: The only full modern reference grammar; its 56-page phonology chapter covers tone, syllable and mora and is where a statement on stress (or its absence) would be, if any exists.

sources.citation: Omachonu, Gideon Sunday. 2001. Igala Phonetics and Phonology: An Overview. MA thesis, University of Nigeria, Nsukka. 139 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Dedicated phonetics/phonology overview by a native-speaker linguist; the most likely place for an explicit suprasegmental section (tone vs. stress).

sources.note: Cited by Adeniyi 2017 and Are & Akinola 2017 as the standard source on Igala tone (contour-tone formation); may contain a prosodic overview.

sources.note: Full-length phonology (historical, but with a synchronic sketch) by a UCLA phonetician; likely to state explicitly that Igala has tone and no stress.

CrossRef record confirms a 56-page phonology chapter; ABC blurb says the book 'establishes 28 phonemic consonants and 7 vowels, as well as lexical and grammatical tones'. Google Books legacy full-text probe (q=<word> inauthor:Ejeba): 'syllable', 'mora', 'tone' each return the grammar; 'stress', 'stressed', 'accent', 'intonation', 'prominence' return nothing - weak indication that the grammar contains no stress s…
